sentences.text: The generic name Lythronax combines Greek words meaning gore and king.
Its specific name argestes honors a southwest wind named by Homer, referencing the fossil's location in North America.
This animal was estimated to reach lengths between 5 and 8 meters and weigh from 0.5 to 2.5 tonnes.
Its frontmost teeth were the largest in the skull, with the longest measuring almost 13 centimeters.
The single known specimen was found in 2009 within the Wahweap Formation of the Grand Staircase–Escalante National Monument in Utah.
Paleontologist Mark A. Loewen and colleagues designated specimen UMNH VP 20200 as the holotype for Lythronax argestes in 2013.
The rocks holding these fossils are estimated to be 81.49 million years old, with an uncertainty range of 81.86 to 81.45 million years.
Lythronax possessed forward-facing eyes that offered depth perception, likely aiding in pursuit or ambush hunting.
It was likely the largest predator within its ecosystem.
Contemporary vertebrates included freshwater fish, bowfins, rays, sharks, turtles like Compsemys, crocodilians, and lungfish.
Numerous mammals also inhabited the region, including multituberculates, cladotherians, marsupials, and placental insectivores.
Lythronax belongs to the family Tyrannosauridae, a group of large-bodied coelurosaurs.
Based on its stratigraphic position, it is considered the oldest known tyrannosaurid.
According to Loewen and colleagues, this species was more closely related to Tarbosaurus and Tyrannosaurus than to Daspletosaurus and Teratophoneus.
Lythronax lived during the Campanian stage in the Western Interior Basin.
Its environment featured lakes, floodplains, and rivers flowing eastward.
Evidence suggests the climate was wet and seasonal.
The discovery of Lythronax indicates that forward-directed eye orbits appeared in tyrannosauroids by at least 80 million years ago.
Gregory S. Paul suggested that Lythronax argestes might belong to the genus Tyrannosaurus, arguing that derived tyrannosaurids are oversplit.
It is debated whether differences in phylogenetic results stem from an over-weighting of certain features by Loewen and colleagues.
It is debated whether Tyrannosaurus originated from Asian tyrannosaurids or from southern Laramidian tyrannosaurids.
Brusatte and Carr proposed that Tyrannosaurus was an invasive migrant species from Asia that spread across Laramidia during the Maastrichtian.
